column2: Do you not remember, in the heedless confusion of deeds done and undone, good and bad? Lay up the one treasure alone.
Before old age, destroying strength, form and beauty, wears out your body, lay up the one treasure alone.
Before the Ender pierces the body with arrows of disease and forcibly ends life, practise great austerity.
Before the dreadful wolves that haunt human bodies rush upon you from every side, strive in the practice of merit.
Before you see darkness alone, hasten, before you behold golden trees on the mountain's head.
Before bad company and enemies with friendly faces make you waver in sight, strive, son, for the highest.
Gather that wealth which has no fear from king or thief, and which, being dead, does not leave you.
There it is not divided among one another by their deeds; what is each one's own dowry, that alone he enjoys there.
Let that be given, son, by which one lives in the other world; gather for yourself that imperishable and fixed wealth.
Before the great man's barley is ripened, while the barley is still unripe, you are quickly led away.
Neither mother, father nor kin, nor a praised and dear person follows one going alone into the pit.
Whatever deed alone, good or bad, one has done by oneself, that is his dowry as he goes to the other world.
Heaps of gold and jewels gathered by good and bad means do not help him on the dissolution of the body.
For the deeds done and undone by you who go to the other world, there is no witness among men here equal to the self.
Empty of the human body he goes to the other world; look with the eye of wisdom, for it is seen on every side.
Here fire, sun and wind, three dwelling in the body, are the witnesses of that man, seeing dharma.
As in the nights, touching all sides and all doors, in concealed and manifest conduct, guard your own dharma alone.
On a path with many bandits, guarded by fearsome and ugly ones, let your own deed alone be guarded; one's own deed goes there.
There it is not divided among one another by one's own deed; as done, the fruit born of one's deed alone is enjoyed.
As troops of apsarases, together with great sages, gain fruit and happiness, so, through deeds, these who go as they like in celestial cars gain it.
As here whatever good has been done by the sinless and the self-possessed, so men of pure birth attain it.
They go to the highest goal, the world of Prajapati, of Brihaspati, of Shatakratu, by the bridges of householder dharma.
We can tell it in thousands of ways, in many ways; again, the lord, without the barley, does not remove the confusion of the unwise.
Two thousand years have gone; you are fixed, the twenty-fifth; build up a store of dharma, for your age is passing.
Before that Ender makes the heedless one's restraint like a cow's mouth, rise as you have taken it, hasten in guarding dharma.
When you go behind and ahead alone, what use is the self, or another, to one who will go to that state?
What comes to the good who go alone to the other world, lay up that great treasure against fear, for the next life.
The lord, unattached, carries off family, root and kin; he has no hinderers; make a store of dharma.
This illustration, son, I have given here, approved by me; it is set out by inference from one's own sight; do accordingly.
He who by his own deed gives wealth to whomever, through qualities born of ignorance and delusion, is joined to a hundred, one alone.
Let what you have heard be effective for you, doing good deeds; that alone is the sight here, grateful and joined with meaning.
This is a binding rope, the delight of one living in a village; having cut it, the virtuous go; the wicked do not cut it.
What use to you is wealth, what are kin, what are sons, my boy, you who will die? Seek the self that has entered the cave; where have all your grandfathers gone?
Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's in the forenoon; for who knows whose army of death will encamp today?
Having followed to the edge of the cremation ground, kinsmen turn back, having cast the man into the fire, relatives and friends too.
Keep to your left the unbelievers, the merciless, men set in sinful minds; wishing the highest, be confident and unwearied.
With the world thus struck and pressed hard by time, resorting to great fortitude, practise dharma with your whole self.
Then the man who rightly knows this means of insight, having rightly practised dharma, prospers here and in the next world.
For those who know, there is no death in the breaking of the body, nor destruction on a well-kept path; the wise man increases dharma; he who falls from dharma is bewildered.
Of the two set on the path of action by their own deeds, the doer gains the fruit duly; one of poor deeds goes to hell; one who has crossed dharma goes to heaven.
Having gained the hard-won human state, the stepping-stone to heaven, so should one steady oneself that one does not fall again.
Him whose mind, following the path to heaven, does not stray, they call a doer of meritorious deeds, not to be mourned by friends and kin.
He whose understanding is not harmed and holds to its resolves, who has made room for himself in heaven, has no great fear.
Those born in the penance-groves and dying there itself, not knowing the enjoyment of desires, have a lesser dharma.
But he who, giving up enjoyments, practises austerity with his body has gained nothing; that fruit I hold in high regard.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, hundreds of sons and wives, past and to come: whose are they, or whose are we?
You have no business with them, nor have they with you; they have gone by their own deeds, and you too will go.
In this world even a stranger becomes kin to the rich; but for the poor, kin vanish while they live.
A man gathers evil deeds out of regard for his wife; from this he gets suffering, here and hereafter alike.
See the world of the living as a hollow by your own deeds; do that, my son, which has been declared in full.
Having seen this and entered the field of action, one who seeks the other world should do good acts.
With months and seasons as its names, a revolving wheel, with the sun as fire, and day and night as fuel, with steadiness in one's own deed as witness of the fruit, Time cooks beings by force.
What is the use of wealth that one neither gives nor enjoys? Of strength that does not hinder enemies? Of learning by which one does not practise dharma? Of a self that is not master of its senses?
Hearing this beneficial speech of Dvaipayana, Shuka went forth, leaving his father, the teacher of liberation.
[Yudhishthira said:] On whom did the ascetic Vyasa beget Shuka? We do not know his mother, nor the foremost birth of that great soul.
And how did the mind of a mere boy go to subtle knowledge, as in no other here, nor in any second?
I wish to hear this at length, O greatly radiant one; I am not sated while hearing this highest nectar.
The greatness, the yoga of the self and the wisdom of Shuka: tell me that in due order, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] Not by years, nor by grey hairs, nor by wealth, nor by kin did the sages make dharma; he who is learned in the Vedas is great among us.
All this you ask me about has austerity as its root, Pandava; by restraining the senses, austerity comes to be, not otherwise.
By indulgence of the senses a man doubtless incurs fault; by restraining them alone he gains success.
Of a thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred Vajapeyas, dear one, no fruit is equal to a fraction of yoga.
Entering himself by yoga, intent on the dharma of yoga, bearing austerity, he practised penance for the sake of a son, best of Kurus.
May my son be measured in power with fire, earth, water, wind and space: so he resolved.
Then with that resolve, hard to attain for the unpractised, he sought the lord of gods, established in the highest austerity.
The lord is said to have stood a hundred years living on wind, worshipping Mahadeva of many forms, the lord of Uma.
There were all the Brahmarishis and the divine sages, the guardians of the world and the Sadhyas with the Vasus, around the lord of the world,
the Adityas and the Rudras, the sun and moon, the Maruts and the wind, the oceans and the rivers,
the Ashvins, the divine Gandharvas, Narada and Parvata, the Gandharva Vishvavasu, the Siddhas and troops of apsarases.
There Rudra Mahadeva shone, wearing a lovely garland made of karnikara flowers, like the moon with its light.
In that lovely divine forest, thronged with gods and divine sages, the sage stood in supreme yoga, bent on a son.
His colour did not fade nor did weariness arise in him; to all three worlds that seemed wonderful.
His matted locks, blazing like the tip of Vaishvanara's flame, were seen shining in him, joined with boundless energy.
The blessed Markandeya told me this; he always related to me the deeds of the god here.
Those very locks of Krishna, kindled by that austerity, shine to this day, dear one, fire-coloured, of the great soul.
With such austerity, and with devotion, Bharata, Maheshvara, pleased in spirit, made up his mind.
The blessed Tryambaka, smiling as it were, said to him: "Such a son shall be born to you, Dvaipayana.
As fire, as wind, as earth, as water and as space, so shall your great son be pure.
Of that nature, of that mind, of that self, having that as refuge, he will cover the three worlds with splendour and win unique fame."
Then, O king, the blessed sage saw the apsara named Ghritachi, bearing supreme beauty with her own radiance.
Seeing the apsara, the blessed Vyasa was suddenly bewildered by desire in that forest, Yudhishthira.
And Ghritachi, having then made Vyasa's mind agitated with love, became a parrot, great king, and approached.
Seeing that apsara covered in another form, he was followed by the bodily passion that pervades all limbs.
Restraining with great fortitude the desire in his heart, the sage Vyasa could not hold back his spreading mind; and because of what was to be, he was carried away by Ghritachi's body.
While the sage strove to restrain himself, wishing to make fire, his seed suddenly fell upon the fire-stick itself.
With unhesitating mind, that best of twice-born, the Brahmarishi, churned the fire-stick just as it was, and in it Shuka was born, O king.
As the fire-stick was being churned, Shuka of great austerity was born, a supreme sage, a great yogi, born from the womb of the fire-stick.
The Gandharva Vishvavasu, and Tumburu and Narada, and the Gandharvas Haha and Huhu praised Shuka's birth.
There the guardians of the world assembled, with Shakra at their head, and the gods, divine sages and Brahmarishis.
The wind rained down all kinds of divine flowers there, and the world, moving and unmoving, became delighted.
The great soul of great radiance himself, with the goddess, joyfully, as soon as the sage's son was born, duly initiated him.
To him Shakra, lord of gods, gladly gave a divine and wonderful-looking water-pot and garments, O lord.
Swans, hundred-petalled birds, cranes by the thousand, parrots and others circled around him, Bharata.
The radiant son of the fire-stick, having gained that divine birth, the wise one stayed right there, a student keeping his vows, composed.
As soon as he was born, the Vedas with their secrets and compendia approached him, great king, as they had his father.
He chose Brihaspati, who knew the Vedas, Vedangas and commentaries, as his teacher, great king, contemplating dharma alone.
Having studied all the Vedas with their secrets and compendia, and the Itihasa entire, and the treatises of kingship, O lord,
and having given the teacher his fee, the great sage returned and began fierce austerity as a composed student.
Even in boyhood he was a great ascetic, worthy of counsel and honour by gods and sages, by knowledge and austerity alike.
But his mind, ruler of men, did not delight in the three stages rooted in the householder's life, as he beheld the dharma of liberation.
[Shuka said:] May the blessed one, skilled in the dharmas of liberation, tell me how the highest peace of my mind may come about, lord.
Hearing his son's words, the supreme sage said to him: "Study, my son, liberation and the various dharmas.
By his father's command Shuka, best of knowers of Brahman, learned the whole treatise of yoga and the Sankhya too, Bharata.
When Vyasa thought his son, joined with the glory of Brahman and with power like Brahman, skilled in the knowledge of liberation,
he then said: "Go to Janaka, lord of Mithila; he will tell you in full, specially, the purpose of liberation.
By his father's command he went to Janaka the king of Mithila, to ask about the end of dharma and the final refuge of liberation.
And he was told: "Go by the human way, unpuffed; do not go by power, through the sky.
Go with simplicity, not by a path seeking comfort; do not look for special distinctions, for distinctions belong to the attached.
That king, skilled in dharma and learned in the treatise of liberation, is my sacrificial patron; whatever he says should be done without hesitation."
Thus told, the righteous-souled sage went to Mithila on foot, though able to cross the earth with its oceans through the sky.
He crossed mountains, passed rivers and lakes, forests filled with many beasts of prey, of various kinds,
passing in order Meru and the Hari-varsha, the two regions, and the Himavat region, he reached the land of Bharata.
Seeing various lands inhabited by Chinas and Hunas, he came, reflecting, to this land of Aryavarta.
Taking his father's word and reflecting on that very purpose, he crossed the road, a sky-goer like a sky-goer.
Shuka, seeing, did not see the lovely towns, the prosperous cities and the varied jewels.
Passing the lovely gardens and shrines and holy bathing-places along the road,
in no long time he reached Videha, guarded by the righteous king, the great-souled Janaka.
There he saw many villages with abundant food and drink, herdsmen's settlements, prosperous, crowded with many herds of cattle,
rich in rice and barley, visited by swans and cranes, adorned with hundreds of beautiful lotus-ponds.
Having crossed Videha, frequented by prosperous people, he reached the lovely and very rich groves of Mithila.
Crowded with elephants, horses and chariots, full of men and women, he passed it seeing and not seeing, unshaken.
Carrying that burden in mind and reflecting on that very purpose, delighting in the self, serene, he reached Mithila.
Reaching its gate and stopped by the gatekeepers, he stood absorbed in meditation; then freed, as he was known, he entered.
Reaching the royal road thronged with prosperous people, and reaching the king's abode, he entered without fear.
There too the harsh-spoken gatekeepers stopped him, and Shuka stood there without anger.
Not scorched by the heat of the road, nor wearied by hunger and thirst, he neither faltered nor drooped, nor withdrew from the sun.
One of those gatekeepers, full of grief, seeing Shuka standing like the sun at noon,
honoured him duly, saluted him with joined palms, and then admitted him to the second court of the royal house.
Seated there, dear one, Shuka, thinking only of liberation, of great radiance, was equal in shade and in sun.
After a moment the king's minister came to him with joined palms and then led him into the third court of the royal house.
There was a great grove joined to the inner apartments, like Chaitraratha, lovely, with well-divided waters and pleasure-places, with flowering trees.
Having shown Shuka that excellent grove, the minister pointed him to a fitting seat and went out again.
Then women of beautiful dress, fair-hipped and lovely to see, wearing fine red garments and ornaments of refined gold,
skilled in talk and conversation, expert in dance and song, speaking with a smile first, equal to apsarases in beauty,
skilled in the service of desire, knowing feelings, knowing all things: about fifty women, the foremost of courtesans, ran up to him.
Receiving him with water for the feet and the rest, honouring him with worship, they satisfied him with good food suited to place and time.
When he had eaten, dear one, they showed him one by one that grove of the inner apartments, very lovely, O Bharata.
Playing, laughing and singing, they all, knowing the heart, waited on Shuka of noble nature.
But the pure-souled son of the fire-stick, free of the three doubts, doing the three works, master of his senses, with anger conquered, neither rejoiced nor was angry.
Those excellent women gave him a divine couch and seat, fit for the best, adorned with jewels, spread with rich coverings.
Having washed his feet and worshipped at twilight, Shuka sat on the holy seat, reflecting on that very purpose.
In the first part of the night the lord remained there absorbed in meditation, and in the middle of the night took sleep as was proper.
Then, rising after a moment and performing purification, the wise one, surrounded by women, followed meditation.
In this manner Krishna's son, unfallen, passed the rest of that day and that night in the king's house, Bharata.
Placing a seat in front, and various jewels, taking the guest-water on his head, he went up to the son of Puru.
Taking that seat adorned with many jewels, spread with rich coverings, auspicious on all sides and splendid,
held by the priest and touched with his hand, the king gave it, greatly honoured, to the teacher's son Shuka.
Seated there, he duly honoured Krishna's son by the scriptures; he first offered water for the feet, then the guest-offering and a cow; and Shuka accepted that worship with mantras, as prescribed.
Accepting that worship from Janaka, the best of the twice-born, permitting the cow and honouring the king,
the greatly radiant Shuka asked the king, king of kings, of his unfailing welfare and health, and that of his attendants.
Permitted by him, he sat with his followers; the king, of noble nature and birth, stood on the ground with joined palms.
Having asked Vyasa's son of welfare and health, the king asked: "What is the reason for your coming?"

I, by my father's command, have come here to ask you; therefore, best of upholders of dharma, you ought to tell me truly.
mahabharata:12:313.13	What is a brahmana to do here, and what is the aim of liberation, and what is its nature? And how is liberation to be achieved, by knowledge or by austerity?
[Janaka said:] "Hear what a brahmana must do here from birth onward. Having had the sacred thread, dear one, he should be devoted to the Veda.
With austerity, service to the teacher and celibacy, O lord, he should be free of debt to the gods and ancestors, and without envy.
Having studied the Vedas in restraint and given the teacher's fee, the twice-born, receiving permission, should then return home.
Returned, he should live restrained in the householder's life with his wife, without envy, duly keeping the sacred fires.
Having begotten sons and grandsons, he should live in a forest hermitage, worshipping those same fires by the scripture, fond of guests.
Knowing dharma, having duly placed the fires in the self in the forest, free of the pairs, with a self free of passion, he should dwell in the hermitage of Brahman."
[Shuka said:] "When knowledge and realisation have arisen, direct and eternal in the heart, what need is there of living in the stages or in the forests?
This I ask you; you ought to tell it; tell me truly, as the meaning of the Veda is, lord of men."
[Janaka said:] "Without knowledge and realisation there is no attainment of liberation; without connection with a teacher, attainment of knowledge is not remembered.
The teacher is the boatman, knowledge is called the boat here; having understood and done what was to be done, one who has crossed should leave both.
For the non-destruction of the worlds and of rites, the dharma of the four stages, as told, has been practised by earlier ones.
By this sequence of practice, through deeds in many births, having done good and bad action, what is called liberation is gained here.
Through the causes that have come about in many wombs of rebirth, the pure self reaches liberation in the first stage.
Having reached it, for one liberated, who has seen the aim and is wise, what purpose could there be in the three stages for one seeking the highest?
He should always avoid the faults of rajas and tamas, and, standing on the path of sattva, see the self by the self.
Seeing the self in all beings and all beings in the self, he is not stained, like a water-creature in water.
Like a bird rising above its perch, he attains the endlessness of the beyond; leaving the body, freed, free of the pairs, he has gone to peace.
Here hear the verses sung of old by King Yayati, which are held by twice-born skilled in the treatises of liberation, dear one.
The light is in the self, not elsewhere, and delights there itself; that can be seen by oneself with a well-composed mind.
When one fears nothing from another and none fears him, and he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
When he does not harbour evil towards any being in deed, mind or speech, then he attains Brahman.
Joining the self with austerity, casting off bewildering envy, giving up desire and greed, he then attains Brahman-hood.
When in what is heard and seen, and toward all beings, he becomes equal and free of the pairs, then he attains Brahman.
When he sees praise and blame with equality, gold and iron, pleasure and pain alike,
cold and heat, gain and loss, dear and undear, life and death, then he attains Brahman.
As the tortoise, having stretched out its limbs, draws them in again, so a mendicant must restrain his senses by the mind.
As a house wrapped in darkness is seen by a lamp, so the self can be beheld by the lamp of understanding.
I see all this in you, best of the wise; and whatever else is to be known, you know in truth.
You are known to me, Brahmarishi, to have reached the end of objects, by your teacher's grace and by your own training.
By his grace, great sage, this divine knowledge has arisen in me too; by that you are known to me.
Your realisation is greater, your goal is greater, your lordship is greater, and you do not understand that.
Through childishness or doubt or fear, those born without release, even when realisation has arisen, do not reach that goal.
By pure resolve, with doubt cut by those like me, loosing the knots of the heart, one reaches that goal.
You, in whom realisation has arisen, steady in understanding and free of greed, reach the Supreme, Brahmana, by resolve alone.
You have no distinction in pleasure and pain, no greed, no eagerness for dance and song, no passion arises in you.
You have no attachment to kin, no fear in fears; I see you, great-souled, with clod, stone and gold alike.
I too see you, and other wise men do, standing on the supreme path, imperishable and free of ill.
The fruit that a brahmana has here, and the aim of liberation, whatever its nature, in that you already stand, Brahmana; what else do you ask?"
[Bhishma said:] Having done what was to be done, happy and calm, he went silently northward, toward Mount Shaishira, as a companion of Matarishvan.
At that very time the divine sage Narada came to the Himalaya, frequented by Siddhas and Charanas, to see it.
It was thronged with troops of apsarases, resounding with the noise of song, with groups of kinnaras and with bhringarajas,
with madgu birds, khanjaritas, with colourful jivajivakas, with peacocks of many colours shining with hundreds of cries, with flocks of royal swans and delighted cuckoos,
where Garuda, king of birds, always goes, where the four guardians of the world and the gods with the troops of sages always come together for the good of the world,
where Vishnu, the great soul, practised austerity for a son, and where Kumara in boyhood hurled the dwellers of heaven,
and, scorning the three worlds, cast his spear to the ground; where Skanda, hurling this speech, said to the world:
Is there any other greater than I, whom brahmanas hold dearer, who is a friend of brahmanas, a second hero in the three worlds?
And Agni accepted that king's daughter Sudarshana by the rite seen in the Veda, like a stream of wealth at a sacrifice.
Take comfort, lord of gods; I shall never take the ladle at a sacrifice for a mortal. Hear this word of mine.
[Vaishampayana said:] Then the righteous king, the Pandava, gently wiped his chest and face with his cold-watered hand.
Karkotaka, Vasuki and Takshaka, Prithushravas, Varuna and Kunjara, Mishri, Shankha, Kumuda, Pundarika, and the great-souled naga Dhritarashtra,
Formerly you were Parikshit's, towards Dvaitavana, for the sake of the fire-sticks, and you crossed that too.
